raw_response.adversarial_critique: Claude's Table 2 numbers, negative raw sign, inverse polarity ('higher = worse'), and 'Favourable' direction accurately summarize Bruggink's headline test across both unweighted Model 1 (-4.6 pp, t = -4.58, p < 0.01) and bill-weighted Model 2 (-4.24 pp, t = -2.71, p < 0.01; Table 2, p. 236), after the A26 ruling aligned the exposure pole with state PUC regulation rather than local municipal control. However, coding this study cleanly under 'affordability' ('ai_scope_check_2026-10-14 = passed') glosses over a major construct-validity gap: the outcome is an imputed Harberger allocative deadweight loss triangle (W = (1/2)Qe(P - LRMC)^2/P divided by residential revenue PQ; pp. 231, 236) among already-connected municipal customers, and the paper never reports whether residential water prices (P) or annual bills (PQ, illustrated at $40-$80/year on p. 237) are actually lower in state-regulated utilities. Bruggink explicitly cautions that residential peak capacity demand reflects discretionary 'lawn sprinkling demand' and that setting P = LRMC under economies of scale would require an external subsidy whose economic cost is ignored (p. 238), meaning lower Harberger loss does not automatically translate into household bill affordability. Furthermore, the dossier's effect_sizes.csv falsely labels the estimate 'adjusted' (underpinning an overly generous 'Low concern' JBI cross-sectional risk-of-bias rating): OLS Equations [1], [3], and [6] (pp. 233-235) and Foster and Beattie's Table 1 regional elasticity slopes (Bp, p. 232) only construct the outcome variable, whereas Table 2 is a completely unadjusted two-sample t-test comparing 27 utilities in five states (Maine, Indiana, Montana, West Virginia, Wisconsin; Note 9, p. 239) against 88 utilities elsewhere—mechanically confounding state regulation with lower imputed Midwest demand elasticities (|Bp| = 0.0804 vs. up to 0.2686 in Western regions). Finally, exposure_full and comparator_full misstate the unit of observation as 'Residential customers' when n = 88 and n = 27 are municipally-owned water utilities (residential customer class aggregates).

raw_response.numerical_check_note: All numerical estimates, standard errors, group sample sizes, differences, t-ratios, and significance levels in Claude's SWiM row and dossier match Table 2 (PDF p. 8 / p. 236) and text (pp. 237-238): Model 1 locally-regulated 9.6% (SE .583, n = 88) vs. state-regulated 5.2% (SE .818, n = 27), printed difference -4.6 pp, t = -4.58 (p < 0.01, one-tailed; 46% lower relatively on p. 238); Model 2 locally-regulated 10.39% (SE .786; rounded to 10.4% on p. 237) vs. state-regulated 6.15% (SE 1.35), difference -4.24 pp, t = -2.71 (p < 0.01, one-tailed; 41% lower relatively on p. 238). The dossier's regex check missed 0.818 only because Table 2 omits the leading zero and OCR misread the closing parenthesis as '(.8181' (similarly printing '-2,71*' and 'n - 88' / 'n - 27'). Note that in the source paper itself, 5.2 - 9.6 = -4.4 pp rather than the printed -4.6 pp, though -4.6 / sqrt(0.818^2 + 0.583^2) = -4.58 confirms -4.6 pp is the unrounded difference. Two non-numerical metadata errors appear in the dossier/effect_sizes.csv: (1) n = 88 and n = 27 are municipal utilities (residential class aggregates), not individual residential customers; and (2) Table 2 is an unadjusted two-group t-test, not a covariate-adjusted comparison.
raw_response.polarity_or_orientation_issue: Outcome polarity is correctly coded as 'higher = worse' (larger Harberger monopoly welfare loss % reflects greater supra-marginal-cost pricing distortion), so combining the negative raw difference (-4.6 pp for state-regulated minus locally-regulated utilities) with 'as reported' exposure orientation yields 'Favourable' for state PUC regulation (consistent with Family C regulatory oversight and Note 23's 'regulated' vs. 'unregulated' terminology). As noted in coding_note, orienting the exposure around local municipal autonomy/decentralization (as effect_sizes.csv did prior to the A26 swap) flips the contrast to +4.6 pp ('Unfavourable'). Substantively, equating lower allocative deadweight loss with 'improved affordability' is also tenuous because group tariff/bill levels are unreported and marginal-cost pricing under economies of scale requires unmodeled subsidies (p. 238).
